Notes: Earliest documented Jewish presence (basis of Year Established -125): jar fragment/ostracon SEPP0100 from Sepphoris inscribed in Hebrew script (אפמלס לש), dated by IIP to the second half of the 2nd c. BCE (150-100 BCE; midpoint -125, c.); ed. J. Naveh, IEJ 52 (2002). Indicates Hebrew-writing (Jewish) residents in the early Hasmonean period; no count.

Same ostracon (2nd c. BCE) interpreted by Chancey & Meyers (BAR 26:4, 2000) as a Hebrew transliteration of Greek epimeletes ('manager/overseer'), possibly a Jewish officeholder, pointing to 'a well-developed Jewish community at Sepphoris at least as early as the Hasmonean period (141-37 B.C.E.)'. Organized community; no count. Year c. (late 2nd c. BCE).

Josephus, Antiquities 13.338 (13.12.5): Ptolemy (Lathyrus) 'tried to take Sepphoris' but lost many men, then fought Alexander Jannaeus at the Jordan. Sepphoris was a Hasmonean-held town early in Jannaeus' reign (c. 103-102 BCE). Event; no count.

NEAEHL entry 'Sepphoris': two mikvehs dated to the early 1st c. BCE found on the eastern edge of the western summit (Hasmonean period, c.; year = Hasmonean midpoint -90). Ritual baths attest Jewish residents; no count.

Excavation reports quoted (Meyers et al. 1992; Strange et al. 2006): numerous Hasmonean coins incl. coins of Alexander Jannaeus (103-76 BCE) and a Hasmonean coin with Paleo-Hebrew inscription in domestic loci; 'domestic occupation at the summit of the hill in the Late Hellenistic period'. Year = Jannaeus reign midpoint (c.). Supports Josephus on Sepphoris as a Hasmonean stronghold; no count.

BAS sidebar 'Sepphoris in Ancient History': 'Archaeological evidence indicates the presence of a Jewish community at Sepphoris during the Hasmonean period'; Sepphoris survived Pompey's conquest (63 BCE) as a Hasmonean stronghold. Hasmonean period 140-37 BCE midpoint -90 (c.). Community; no count.

Josephus, Antiquities 14.91 (14.5.4): Gabinius divided the nation into five councils (synedria), 'the fifth at Sepphoris in Galilee' (c. 57-55 BCE). Sepphoris as Jewish administrative centre of Galilee; no count.

Josephus, Antiquities 14.414 (14.15.4): Herod passed on to Sepphoris in a snowstorm while Antigonus's garrison withdrew (winter 39/38 BCE, c.). Sepphoris had been held for the Hasmonean Antigonus; event; no count.

Jewish Encyclopedia 'Joseph (High Priest)': Joseph son of Ellem of Sepphoris was installed by Herod as substitute high priest for one day (Yom Kippur), dated 4 BCE (Josephus, Ant. 17.6.4; Tosefta Yoma 1.4). Individual priest from Sepphoris; attests priestly Jewish residents; no count.

Josephus, Antiquities 17.271 (17.10.5): after Herod's death Judas son of Ezekias gathered men 'about Sepphoris in Galilee', attacked the royal palace there and seized its weapons and money (4 BCE). Event; no count.

Josephus, Antiquities 17.289 (17.10.9; cf. War 2.68): Varus' force 'took Sepphoris, and made its inhabitants slaves, and burnt the city' (4 BCE). Destruction and enslavement event. Population left blank (not 0): Josephus does not state that no Jews remained, and modern scholars note the account may be exaggerated (no clear conflagration layer); the city was rebuilt as a Jewish town by Antipas.

Strange et al. (2006), USF excavations as quoted: destruction of an earlier house on the summit attributed 'probably by Varus at the end of the 1st century B.C.E.' Archaeological echo of the 4 BCE destruction; no count.

Josephus, Antiquities 18.27 (18.2.1): Herod Antipas 'built a wall about Sepphoris... and made it the metropolis of the country' (rebuilding after 4 BCE; year c. -3). Refounding as the capital of Jewish Galilee; no count.

Ronny Reich, 'They Are Ritual Baths', BAR 28:2 (2002): counted 22 stepped and plastered water installations at Sepphoris; the three larger rectangular pools 'almost surely date to the Second Temple period'; most were mikva'ot; 'many mikva'ot means many Jews'. Early Roman midpoint 4 CE (c.). Suggests a large Jewish population; no count.

Sherman, Weiss, Zilberman & Yasur, BASOR 383 (2020): chalkstone vessels (used in Judaea and Galilee from the second half of the 1st c. BCE) were used by 'Sepphoreans', many produced in local Lower Galilee quarries; use continued after 70. Jewish purity practice; early Roman midpoint 4 CE (c.); no count.

Mark A. Chancey, 'The Myth of a Gentile Galilee' (Bible and Interpretation, 2003): first-century Sepphoris 'was one of the biggest towns in Galilee, with between 8000 and 12000 inhabitants' (midpoint 10000); same source: 'All signs point to a predominantly Jewish population' (mikvot, stone vessels, very low pig bones, no 1st-c. pagan dedications). Total population of a predominantly Jewish town per the source. 1st c. CE midpoint = 50.

Chancey & Meyers (BAR 26:4, 2000) as captioned: stone-vessel fragments in the first-century C.E. residential area, paucity of Roman-period pig bones and numerous mikva'ot are three 'ethnic markers' of a predominantly Jewish first-century Sepphoris. 1st c. CE midpoint 50. Presence; no count.

Introduction to Galilee vols. 1-2 (Fortress Press): scholarly total-population estimates for first-century Sepphoris: E. M. Meyers 18000 ('Jesus and His Galilean Context', 59). Population left blank because this source does not state the Jewish share; it also records Horsley's 15000 for Sepphoris and Tiberias combined (regional aggregate). 1st c. CE midpoint 50.

Same Fortress Press introduction: range of estimates for Sepphoris from 'up to 30,000 persons' (J. A. Overman, SBL Seminar Papers 1988: 30000) to a small city of 'around 7,500'; cf. Reed, Archaeology and the Galilean Jesus, 117. Total-population estimates; Population blank (Jewish share not stated in this source). 1st c. CE midpoint 50.

Josephus, War 2.511 (2.18.11): Cestius Gallus 'was received by the strongest city of Galilee, which was Sepphoris, with acclamations of joy' (66 CE). Pro-Roman stance at outbreak of the Great Revolt; no count.

Josephus, Life 30: the people of Sepphoris in agony because 'the Galileans had resolved to plunder it, on account of the friendship they had with the Romans' (alliance with Cestius Gallus, 66 CE). Event; no count.

Wikipedia 'Sepphoris' (citing S. Cohen 2002): Sepphoris did not join the revolt of 66 CE; Cestius Gallus killed about 2000 'brigands and rebels' in the area (casualty count, not Sepphoris' population); Josephus twice failed to take the city. Population blank.

Jewish Encyclopedia 'Sepphoris': during the revolt Sepphoris, 'the most strongly fortified city of the province' and sometimes 'the largest city of Galilee', turned against Josephus; he stormed it and it was 'plundered by his troops' (Vita 67), later repulsed him (Vita 71); inhabitants obtained a Roman detachment from Vespasian (Vita 74; War 3.4.1). c. 66-67 CE. Event; no count.
Josephus, War 3.30: 'the inhabitants of Sepphoris of Galilee met him [Vespasian at Ptolemais], who were for peace with the Romans' (spring 67 CE). Event; no count.
Josephus, War 3.34: Sepphoris was 'the largest city of Galilee, and built in a place by nature very strong' (67 CE). Indicates the largest Jewish town of Galilee; no count.

Jewish Virtual Library 'Zippori': 'The Jews did not join the revolt against Rome in 66 C.E.' and opened the gates to Vespasian; coins minted then name the city Eirenopolis, 'city of peace' (c. 67/68 CE). Jewish community continued through the revolt; no count.
